Description
The International Wolf Center is seeking applicants for the 2027 Dr. L. David Mech fellowship. As an investment in the future of wolf research and science-based wolf education, the Center awards up to two fellowships each year to undergraduate students or recent graduates interested in pursuing careers in natural sciences with an interest in wildlife. Fellowship recipients receive a $6,000 stipend and up to $4,000 in support for field research expenses.

Fellowship Goals
Reduce barriers to allow undergraduate students and recent graduates to directly engage in research and field work.
Encourage students from diverse backgrounds to explore natural sciences/wildlife biology as a profession.
Provide bridge support for early-career researchers prior to graduate school.

Fellowship Award Details
Application opens: November 1, 2026
Application deadline:  February 1, 2027
Fellowships Awarded: March 31, 2027
Term: April 1, 2027 through April 1, 2028
Stipend: $6,000
Research Allowance: up to $4,000 per year

Stipends are meant to support study and research during the tenure of the fellowship. Fellowship recipients are not employees, contracted workers, volunteers or interns of the International Wolf Center and are not covered by IWC’s benefits or insurance. All funds provided, including stipends and research allowances, are subject to tax. Fellows awarded stipends receive a financial summary at the end of each calendar year and are responsible for meeting their own state and federal tax obligations.

Research allowances are for equipment, supplies, research-related travel costs, housing, and other support required to participate in the project. A budget and general justification for these expenses must be included with your application.

A selection team of International Wolf Center staff and board review application materials and select recipients.

Eligibility
Applicant must be a U.S. citizen
Applicants must be either an upper-level student currently enrolled in an undergraduate institution or recently graduated within two years with an undergraduate degree.
Current graduate students, those accepted to graduate school and those already with graduate-level degrees in wildlife biology or a related field are not eligible.

Application Materials:
Purpose Statement: 500-800-word essay focusing on (a) why you are a good candidate through discussion of need for wildlife research experience, financial support and barriers you have faced, (b) your previous career-building experiences and future goals, (c) how you will accomplish the goals of the fellowship program, and (d) your project preference and ability to carry out the project work. Special consideration will be given to Black, Indigenous, and People of Color candidates.
Resume/CV
Budget Proposal: Include financial needs for support during the project. For reference, please see the Sample Budget Proposal. Estimated dollar amounts preferred but not required. You may enlist the help of the research lead to determine needs. If specific expenses are unknown at the time of application, please indicate this in lieu of a budget.
Project Selection: Selection of your preferred project from the provided list.
Reference Letter: An academic or professional reference letter referencing the applicants preferred project and ability to successfully complete the project, emailed by the reference to [email removed] before February 1, 2027.

Application Available At: https://wolf.org/programs/mech-fellowship/

Description
Request for Proposals (RFP) 

Appalachian Headwaters: 2027Graduate Student Field Research Grant 

1. Purpose and Overview 
Appalachian Headwaters invites proposals from master’s or PhD degree seeking students in environmental science, wildlife management, forestry, ecology, natural resource management, geography, or related fields to conduct field-based research in the Central Appalachian region. 
 
To strengthen the connection between academic research and applied restoration, all projects must include at least some components of field research conducted on Appalachian Headwaters property in Greenbrier County, West Virginia. 

2. Organizational Background 
Appalachian Headwaters is a nonprofit based in Lewisburg, WV, dedicated to environmental education and ecological restoration (https://appheadwaters.org/). Major initiatives include: 

Habitat restoration, wildlife, and pollinator garden programs 
Reforestation of degraded pastureland 
A native plant nursery supporting pollinator habitat and restoration plantings 
Environmental education programs for K–12 students and the public 
Citizen science program using wildlife cameras 
Research conducted through this grant program will directly support and expand on one or more of these initiatives.  

3. Appalachian Headwaters Properties 
Research supported through this grant must include a field component on Appalachian Headwaters’ property. Sites include: 

Wood Thrush Park: Mixed use property with educational facilities, trails, gardens, and restoration sites on approximately 150 acres. 
Kestrel Woods: Farmland Restoration Tract: More than 800-acre property, consisting of a 90-acre reforestation project and 750 acres of forest, including early successional to mature (>150-year-old) stands. 
Native Plant Nursery: Native plant propagation facility, producing pollinator-focused species and plants for retail and restoration projects, on approximately 60 acres of old pasture and secondary forest. 

Applicants should propose how research could incorporate one or more of these sites. Final site access and research design will be refined in partnership with Appalachian Headwaters staff if a proposal is selected for funding. 

4. Eligibility Criteria 

Enrollment in a master’s degree or PhD program at an accredited university. 
Relevant fields of study: environmental science, forestry, wildlife management, ecology, geography, or related discipline. 
Work must be conducted in the Appalachian region, with at least part of the research taking place on an Appalachian Headwaters property. 
Faculty advisor endorsement confirming academic standing and project feasibility. 
5. Funding Details 

Award Amount: Up to $3,000 per project 
Number of Awards: Up to 2 applicants per cycle, preference is given to first time applicants 
Funding Period: April–December 2026 
Allowable Expenses: Field equipment, research supplies, travel, data analysis, and community engagement. Tuition and general living expenses are not eligible. *Lodging provided on site, free of charge, at Wood Thrush Park. 
6. Research Focus Areas 

Priority will be given to projects that: 

Utilize Headwaters existing wildlife camera trap and/or invasive plant data sets 
Investigate pollinator biology, native plant ecology, or habitat management on Appalachian Headwaters’ properties. 
Contribute to ongoing research of the wildlife of Central Appalachia, including habitat use, genetics, survival, movement, and other monitoring initiatives  
Advance understanding of forest and watershed restoration on degraded agricultural landscapes. 
Examine ecological or hydrological processes tied to reforestation, invasive species management, or biodiversity. 
Include a community or educational engagement component. 
7. Proposal Components (12 pages max) 

Cover Page – Name, institution, program, advisor, project title. 
Abstract – ~300 words. 
Project Narrative – Background, objectives, methodology, significance, expected outcomes. 
Site Component – Description of how Headwaters’ property will be used as part of the research. Applicants may identify a preferred site type (e.g., forest, pollinator meadow, nursery). Final details will be refined in collaboration with Appalachian Headwaters staff if awarded. 
Timeline – Anticipated schedule of activities. 
Budget Justification – General breakdown of expenses. 
Applicant CV – 2 pages max. 
Faculty Advisor Letter – Statement of support and feasibility. 

8. Review Criteria 
Scientific Merit – Strength of research design and objectives. 
Alignment with Mission – Relevance to Appalachian Headwaters’ restoration and education goals. 
Use of Headwaters’ Property – Clear integration of Appalachian Headwaters’ land into research activities. 
Feasibility – Realistic timeline and budget. 
Community/Educational Impact – Potential to involve or benefit local communities. 

9. Submission Process 

Deadline: Friday, January 31, 2027 (11:59 PM ET) 
Submission: Apply at this link by filling out the application and attaching your Proposal as a PDF. No submissions via email please. If you have questions, you can reach out to Dr. Merri Collins at [email removed] 
Notification of selection: Early March 2026 
Start of Funding: April 2026 

10. Reporting Requirements 
Awardees must:
Deliver a final report (5–10 pages) summarizing findings and relevance to Appalachian Headwaters programs. 
Provide a public-accessible resource (e.g., StoryMap, public talk, community workshop). 
Acknowledge Appalachian Headwaters in academic presentations and publications. 

11. Past Recipients 
Elizabeth Kramer: PhD Student at Ohio University. 2026. “Phylogeography, hybridization, and species delimitation in a complex of cryptic woodland salamanders in central Appalachia.” 
Brian Brillhart: Masters Student at Marshall University. 2026. “Analysis of Black-capped (Poecile atricapillus) and Carolina Chickadee (P. carolinensis) Vocalizations in Allopatric vs. Sympatric Populations.” 
Contact
Dr. Merri Collins

Description
 Canada Excellence Research Chair (CERC) Dr. Deborah McGregor and the research program in Indigenous Planetary Well-being at the University of Calgary are seeking three highly motivated students to contribute to enriched understanding of Indigenous contributions to addressing environmental challenges. Selected applicants will be supported by our research team in applying for admission to the University of Calgary in either the Department of Geography, the Department of Earth, Energy, and the Environment, or the Transdisciplinary Graduate program, depending on specific project and student’s interest. Student will be based out of the University of Calgary, with significant field work with collaborators and partners in locations throughout Ontario and Alberta. 

Application: To apply, please send a CV and cover letter to Carina at [email removed]; applications are rolling with a preferred review deadline of November 20. Please indicate which of the three projects you are interested in and outline your interest and qualifications in your cover letter. 

Projects: 
1.        Indigenous Urban Climate Action, project will involve: 
• Contribute to an original and innovative research program that seeks to document the nature and impact of Indigenous climate action in cities and urban settings (e.g. document urban land stewardship practices) 
• Contribute to understanding how Indigenous climate action influence city and urban climate policy and governance 
• Contribute to an Indigenous urban climate assessment 
• Generate understanding of how Indigenous laws, rights and knowledge can accelerate climate action in cities and urban contexts 
• Generate understanding of the relationships between urban and rural Indigenous led climate action 
• Contribute to supporting Indigenous urban climate priorities 
• Indigenous research methods will be co-designed and produced and may involve: supporting and/or leading interviews; workshops; learning circles, and land-based engagement activities 
• Facilitating knowledge sharing and mobilization and leading community engagement activities and youth engagement activities 
• Contribute to knowledge mobilization activities (multi-media, videos) including organizing speaker series, webinars and workshops 

2.        Indigenous Planetary Well-being, project will involve: 
• Through a collaborative research process, seek to develop the concept of Indigenous planetary well-being 
• Co-develop Indigenous led and community-based well-being frameworks 
• Co-develop Indigenous led and community-based indicators that measure well being 
• Engage with Indigenous knowledge, language, rights, laws and values to develop original indicators of well-being 
• This research may involve leading interviews, workshops, learning circles, Indigenous and community-engaged research methods and land-based activities 
• Facilitate knowledge sharing and mobilization and lead community engagement activities, including with youth 
• Develop skills related to Indigenous research methodologies, knowledge mobilization, and community engagement 

3.        Indigenous Knowledge, Languages and Land-based Practices and Planetary Well-being, project will involve: 
• Advance the revitalization of Indigenous languages, knowledge, laws and land-based practices in support of community well being 
• Co-develop Indigenous led and community-based land-based activities that support the goals of community and planetary well being 
• Co-develop Indigenous led and community-based youth and multi-generational knowledge sharing gatherings 
• Support community led projects that support various aspects of planetary well-being. 
• In collaboration with Indigenous partners, convene Elders, TK holders/practitioners, and youth together to share priorities for future activities that strengthen and restore relationships to the Earth 
• Facilitate knowledge sharing and mobilization and lead community engagement activities, including with youth 
• Develop skills related to Indigenous research methodologies, knowledge mobilization, and community engagement 

Qualifications: 
• Indigenous cultural competency, with experience working with Indigenous communities and/or organizations 
• Undergraduate and/or master's degree in environmental science/studies, health, Indigenous studies, education, urban studies, or related fields 
• Experience with Indigenous research approaches and methodologies and/or community-engaged methods is an asset 
• Experience and skills in literature review and synthesis, writing, qualitative data analysis, and academic writing are assets 
• Excellent communication skills and an interest in knowledge sharing/mobilization 
• Experience coordinating multi-generational gatherings and working with youth are assets 

Contact
Carina Burroughs

 Description 

I am seeking one highly motivated student to join my research group in the Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Sciences (NRES) at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign. Start date will be mid-May 2027. 

During the summer of 2027, the student will analyze a long-term passive acoustic monitoring dataset to determine presence/absence for T & E bat species in National Park Service units in the Upper Midwest and visit the NPS units with Dr. O’Keefe to evaluate the available habitat. During the following academic year, the student will develop distribution models for T & E bats using habitat layers. At present, there is only one year of funding available but there is the potential for a second year of funding that would enable mistnetting surveys to validate GIS models. If the funding is not renewed, the student will be supported through teaching assistantships or fellowships during the second academic year. This study is funded by and will be conducted in collaboration with the National Park Service. Results will inform policy on conservation practices to enhance and protect habitat for federally endangered bats. 

Minimum Qualifications 

Applicants should have a BS degree in biology, ecology, wildlife, or another related discipline. Preferred qualifications include strong quantitative and analytical skills, field research experience, and a competitive GPA. Excellent writing and verbal communication skills, a strong work ethic, and the ability to both work independently and contribute to a research team will also be beneficial. A valid driver’s license is also required. 

Preferred Experience 

Experience with identifying bat calls, processing bat acoustic data in standard software packages, working with large amounts of data, and developing maps in GIS. 

How to Apply 

If interested, please send an email to Dr. Joy O’Keefe ([email removed]) by November 23, 2026 with the following combined into one PDF with your last name in the file name: CV, undergraduate transcripts (unofficial are sufficient), statement of interest addressing minimum qualifications and preferred experience for this project, and contact information for three references. 

Contact
Joy O'Keefe

James Beasley, Travis DeVault, and Jessy Patterson are seeking three highly motivated students with strong academic credentials to join our team and pursue PhD degrees in wildlife ecology at the University of Georgia. Summary: Seeking a motivated MS student to lead research on the breeding ecology of Eastern Bluebirds (Sialia sialis) at Arkansas Tech University. The project will utilize an established array of 120 Eastern Bluebird nest boxes, where the student will continue collecting data for long-term population monitoring while also developing new research questions using data unique to their project. Beyond this core monitoring, the specific research focus is somewhat flexible, and the student will be able to tailor it to match their interests. The faculty advisor (Dr. Doug Barron – https://douglasbarron.weebly.com/) has experience monitoring reproductive success of wild birds and using behavior, genetics, hormones, and disease monitoring to generate a more comprehensive understanding of avian ecology. The student will be encouraged to incorporate some combination of these approaches to develop a multidisciplinary thesis.
 This research will be the focus of the student’s thesis for a Master of Science in Fisheries and Wildlife Science at Arkansas Tech University. ATU is the third-largest university in the state, with an enrollment of approximately 10,000 students. The Russellville campus, located in the scenic Arkansas River Valley between the Ozark and Ouachita Mountains, is about an hour from the capital city of Little Rock and boasts a charming blend of historic and modern architecture, including beautiful grounds and green spaces. For more information about the Fisheries and Wildlife Science program and the MS degree, visit https://www.atu.edu/programs/?id=fisheries-wildlife-science-ms.
 Salary: This year-round position is supported by a teaching assistantship that includes a full tuition waiver and a stipend of $14,000 per year. Teaching duties occur during the fall and spring semesters only; summers are dedicated to field research. Beyond assistantship duties, the student is expected to devote full-time effort to coursework and thesis research. The position is expected to last for 2.5 years, contingent on satisfactory performance and academic progress. 
 Start Date: Between January 1–11, 2027. 
 Qualifications: Applicants must meet the requirements of the Graduate College and have completed a bachelor’s degree in biology, wildlife science, or a related field by the start date. Applicants must also have a good driving record (capable of operating a state vehicle) and must pass a background check. 
 The ideal candidate will exhibit a passion for avian ecology and will have experience with associated field techniques. Comfort with basic laboratory techniques and experience with genetic or physiological assays are a plus but are not required; lab skills can be taught to a student who is willing to learn.
 Required:
·         BS in Biology, Fisheries and Wildlife, or related field
 Preferred Field Experience (in order of importance):
·         One year of field experience
·         Mist netting and bird banding
·         Ornithology coursework
·         Nest searching and/or monitoring
 Preferred Laboratory Experience (in order of importance):
·         Basic laboratory techniques (e.g., pipetting, use of lab equipment)
·         Genetics, endocrinology, entomology, or disease ecology coursework
·         Conducting lab assays (e.g., PCR, EIA)
 Application Process: Applications will be reviewed as they are received, and the position will be filled once a qualified candidate is selected. Applicants are encouraged to apply promptly to ensure consideration.
 To apply, send a single PDF file that includes: 1) cover letter detailing your interest, qualifications, and available start date, 2) resume/CV, 3) unofficial transcripts, and 4) contact information for three professional references.
 Email materials to Dr. Doug Barron at [email removed] with the subject line “Eastern Bluebird MS Assistantship.”
Contact
Doug Barron
[email removed] (preferred contact method)

Description
A PhD studentship is available with Dr. Mitch Weegman in the Department of Biology at the University of Saskatchewan (https://www.ducks.ca/our-work/science/saskatchewan-endowed-chair/). The student will lead a research project on the population ecology of Greenland white-fronted geese, using 40-year data sets to address long-standing questions about drivers of productivity on breeding areas and subpopulation structure. 
 The Greenland white-fronted goose population has continued to decline, from a peak of 35,000 individuals in 1999 to 13,000 individuals in 2025. Productivity is the proximate mechanism for population change and there is continued uncertainty about the degree to which breeding conditions explain variation in productivity. Further, there are ~45 wintering Greenland white-fronted goose flocks (subpopulations) with hypothesized differential demographic structure contributing to the decline and winter range contraction. This PhD studentship has been developed to encourage discovery with anticipated conservation application. Our project goals are to (1) estimate the environmental drivers on breeding areas of productivity in Greenland white-fronted geese, (2) identify structure in survival and reproductive success among 45 wintering Greenland white-fronted goose flocks, and (3) connect population and individual processes linking demography with individual movement and behaviour. The student will use data from thousands of neck-collared individuals and hundreds of GPS-tagged individuals spanning 40 years. This project is an international partnership among National Parks and Wildlife Service (Ireland), Aarhus University (Denmark) and University of Saskatchewan (Canada). There will be substantial additional opportunities for the student to collaborate on other projects in population and movement ecology.
 Prerequisites: Ideal candidates will have an MSc and undergraduate degree in ecology, statistics or a closely related field, and interpersonal skills to lead discussions among collaborators. Preference will be given to those with a strong quantitative background (e.g., experience with Program R, Bayesian methods) and knowledge of migratory bird ecology and management. Students must have a valid driver’s license. The successful applicant will be expected to publish manuscripts in peer-reviewed journals and present papers at scientific meetings.

Description
Graduate Student Opportunities in Urban Animal Cognition and Behavior

Dr. Lauren Stanton | Department of Biological Sciences | Illinois State University
Our research group investigates how animals perceive, learn about, and respond to the challenges and opportunities of living in human-altered environments. We are particularly interested in how individual differences shape wildlife responses to urbanization, influence human-wildlife interactions, and inform coexistence strategies. Looking forward, we will explore how early life experiences, social learning, and cultural transmission further shape animal behavior within and across cities. 

We value partnerships with local communities and recognize community science and public engagement as necessary for not only understanding urban wildlife, but also for the development of effective, equitable approaches to human-wildlife coexistence.


Current Research Opportunities
Graduate students will contribute to an ongoing research program investigating the behavior and ecology of urban raccoons (Procyon lotor) in San Francisco, California. This Bay Area Raccoon Project includes a substantial existing dataset, providing opportunities to investigate questions related to urban animal physiology, health, behavior, cognition, social interactions, movement, and space use.

MS Student (1 position)
The MS student will primarily use existing GPS and biologging data from the Bay Area Raccoon Project for their thesis chapters. This position is particularly well suited to someone interested in asking novel questions by integrating behavioral, animal telemetry, and geospatial datasets.

Potential research topics include individual- and neighborhood-level differences in raccoon activity, health, and risk-taking behavior. The student will work closely with existing collaborators to develop focused, independent research questions using available data. 

Previous research or field experience is expected (see more below). Basic familiarity with R and statistical analyses is required. Additional experience with data analysis, GIS, writing, or science communication is highly desirable. 

 
PhD Student (1 position)
The PhD student will contribute to the existing Bay Area Raccoon Project as part of their dissertation (1–2 chapters), while also developing new, independent investigations (2–3 additional chapters).

Experimental investigations will likely involve additional fieldwork and data collection with raccoons in San Francisco, although opportunities to develop complementary research in Illinois, or with other species, may also be possible. The student will have substantial opportunities to develop independent research questions and pursue work at the intersection of animal behavior, cognition, urban ecology, and human-wildlife interactions.

Experience developing hypotheses, conducting independent research, analyzing data, and communicating findings through presentations or publications is expected. Proficiency in R and experience with statistical analyses are strongly preferred. A publication, manuscript in preparation, or other evidence of research productivity is highly desirable. See below for additional details.

 Who Should Apply?
We are looking for motivated, creative, and collaborative students with demonstrated experience working in research or applied animal settings. Competitive applicants will have some combination of the following:

Research interests: A strong interest in animal cognition, as well as wildlife behavior, movement ecology, urban ecology, and conservation biology.
Research experience: Previous experience in an academic research laboratory, field research project, or a related setting.
Animal experience: Experience working with animals in a field, zoo, wildlife rehabilitation center, veterinary clinic, or similar professional setting.
Quantitative skills: Basic knowledge of R and statistics, with some understanding of multivariate analyses. Experience or interest in developing skills in machine learning, GIS/spatial analyses, and computational approaches to classifying animal behavior from biologging data is highly desirable.
Communication: Strong written, verbal, and interpersonal skills, with the ability to communicate effectively with both academic and non-academic audiences (e.g., when engaging with the public). Website: Home - UGA Deer Lab | Kohl Lab 
Contacts: Marcelo Jorge ([email removed]), Michel Kohl ([email removed]) 
 Description: This position is part of an interdisciplinary project at the University of Georgia (UGA) led by Drs. Kohl and Jorge in the Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources, funded through the Wheatley Interdisciplinary Faculty Seed Grant Program. The project is a collaborative effort involving state wildlife agencies, university partners, and the Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation (RMEF) aimed and understanding how elk habitat management treatments impact nutrition and population vital rates for eastern elk. Through this position you will develop collaborations with agency and RMEF personnel while collecting, cleaning, and analyzing historical treatment data to inform efficient study design and field work logistics planning. This position is not permitted for remote work. Travel will be required to visit field sites. NOTE: This position is only funded for 6 months. 
 Qualifications: Applicants should have an expressed interest in Eastern elk populations, habitat management, genetics, and/or nutrition. Applicants must have completed a Master’s degree in wildlife management or related field and shown a propensity for R coding, GIS, as well as a strong publication record. Exceptional B.S. applicants may be considered with minimum requirements of a Bachelor’s degree GPA >3.0 along with proficiency in R coding, GIS, and statistical analysis. Applicants must be able to pass a UGA background check and driving records check. 
 The Analyst will join a cohesive team of graduate research assistants, postdocs, and P.I.’s within the Kohl Lab and UGA Deer Lab. Because the project will require extensive work with data management and analysis, the student must be comfortable working on a computer developing their statistical analysis and R coding skills. The position start date is negotiable, but must begin January 1, 2027, and funding is available for 6 months with the potential of Ph.D. Assistantship extension contingent on funding and fit beginning August 1 (assuming funding acquisition). For those interested in pursuing a Ph.D. this position provides additional project development time prior to starting the degree program. 
 To be considered for this position, please send a concise cover letter outlining your interests, research background specifically as they relate to this position along with career aspirations. If interested in the possible follow-up PhD position, please note in your cover letter. Also include a sample publication, resume or curriculum vitae; copies of transcripts (unofficial) for all institutions attended; unofficial copies of GRE scores if available; and contact information for 3 professional references (name, email, phone, address) combined into a single PDF file with the file name formatted as lastname_firstname_Data_Analyst to [email removed] and [email removed].  Review of applications will begin Nov 16th . We will be at the wildlife society annual conference in Iowa if you want to discuss the position in person, otherwise feel free to email any question you may have.  
Contact
Marcelo jorge
[email removed] (preferred contact method)

Position Summary:

One Ecologist/Forestry Researcher (Full-time, 40 hrs/week) position available with Colorado State University (CSU) Center for Environmental Management of Military Lands (CEMML). This position is part of CEMML’s Early-Career Development Program, which helps emerging professionals bridge academic learning and career success through hands-on experience, mentorship, and professional development. To learn more visit: Early-Career Development Program - CEMML.


This is a research focus position. The role will use GIS and remotely sensed data, along with Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) data to characterize, map, model and analyze tree species composition and related forest attributes in a tropical environment. This will aid in understanding forest ecosystem disturbance and resilience.


For full consideration, please apply by Monday, November 16, 2026, 11:59 PM (MT). 


Essential Job Duties:

Combine existing spatial data with additional predictor variables developed as needed, with Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) data to characterize and map spatial gradients in tree species composition and related forest attributes.

Evaluate whether mapped outputs or model derived spatial predictors can reduce uncertainties in FIA estimates of tree species basal area, biomass, or related composition metrics through one or more model assisted estimation approaches.

Link mapped species composition outputs to an existing dataset of fire occurrences to characterize tree species composition where fires occurred, including areas where field surveys of tree species are not available.

Develop a comparison of uncertainties in FIA estimates of species basal area, biomass, or related composition metrics when estimates are based only on FIA plots versus when model assisted estimation uses mapped auxiliary information.

Create maps of model derived species composition gradients, or related composition outputs.

Model derived composition values for places where fires occurred, along with related charts that help characterize the species composition of forests where fires occur.


Decision Making:

Determine and develop appropriate model parameters.

Determine appropriate spatial predictor data sets.


Supervision:

Does not supervise.


Conditions of Employment:

Successful completion of CSU’s standard pre-employment background check.

Minimum Qualifications:

PhD in Systems Ecology or related field, including coursework in ecology, ecosystem climatology, statistics, spatial statistics, machine learning, applied bioinformatics, data visualization, geographic information systems and science communication.

One year experience in systems ecology, including work in GIS and remote sensing and FIA plot data in tropical islands of the US.

Experience as first author publishing a refereed journal article in a top journal focused on research typically requiring geospatial data and analysis (e.g., Remote Sensing or Ecological Indicators).

Experience with programming languages including R and Python.


Preferred Qualifications:

Experience developing spatial or statistical models of forest composition, biomass, basal area, or related ecological attributes.

Experience applying model-assisted estimation or other methods that integrate forest inventory data with auxiliary spatial information.

Experience integrating remote sensing, climate, topographic, fire, or other disturbance data in geospatial analyses.

Advanced proficiency using R, Python, and GIS for spatial modeling, uncertainty analysis, visualization, and reproducible workflows.

Experience communicating geospatial research through peer-reviewed publications, technical reports, maps, or presentations.

CEMML ECDP

Full job description

We’re seeking two ecologists to join a dynamic team shaping biodiversity strategy for influential organizations and ambitious nature-forward projects.

These team members will lead the development and implementation of innovative site- and portfolio-scale biodiversity strategies, conduct site assessments and set ecological goals, develop biodiversity-focused recommendations for design and management of sites, and design and conduct biodiversity monitoring projects. The successful candidate will collaborate closely with clients and team members to deliver high-quality, actionable projects and programs that reflect current scientific knowledge, local ecology, regulatory requirements, and client priorities.

We’re looking for one position with substantial consulting/restoration experience and one with strong analytical/landscape ecology experience. Strong candidates from across this spectrum will be considered and candidates don’t need to meet the full list of preferred qualifications.

The position will benefit from client-facing consulting or similar applied experience; strong technical and research background in ecology, landscape ecology, or a closely related field; and well-developed project management abilities, while thriving in a highly collaborative and creative environment. Technical work is likely to include spatial analysis, statistical modeling, literature synthesis, and monitoring design.

You'll translate data and analysis into targets, design guidance, and recommendations that clients and design collaborators can act on. Strong technical skills, clear communication of complex ideas, and the ability to navigate conflicting priorities across multiple stakeholders are essential. You'll develop and manage scopes, budgets, and timelines, while coordinating with project teams and clients. We value candidates who pair scientific depth and creativity with the ability to deliver on schedule.


Minimum Qualifications
